title: DWP's Universal Credit advances machine-learning model saved an estimated £4.4 million from 2022–23 to 2024–25
summary: The National Audit Office reports that DWP's model, in use since May 2022, flags high-risk advance requests for caseworker review, with estimated savings of £4.4 million and about three times the h...
account: The National Audit Office (NAO) published “Tackling benefit overpayments due to fraud and error” on 22 October 2025. It states that since May 2022 the Department for Work & Pensions (DWP) has used a machine learning model. The model flags potentially fraudulent claims for Universal Credit advances. DWP estimates it saved £4.4 million from 2022–23 to 2024–25. The model scores new claims and refers those above a threshold to a caseworker. Decisions are made by DWP staff. DWP cannot disaggregate the model's costs from wider spending on data analytics. The NAO reports DWP's finding that the model is around three times more effective at identifying fraud risk than a randomized control group sample. It reports a median payment delay of one day for referred requests. DWP's July 2025 fairness analysis for 2024–25 showed older claimants (age groups 45 to 54 and above) and non-UK nationals over-referred for review. Fairness analysis was possible on only one of nine protected characteristics. Four further models were in development. Civil Service World (Jim Dunton, 22 October 2025) reported the NAO's warnings on data infrastructure. It quoted Transformation Minister Andrew Western saying that the one machine learning model has made the department significantly more effective.
purpose: Assess the fraud risk of Universal Credit advance requests and refer high-risk requests to a caseworker for review.
system: Universal Credit advances machine learning model

ratings.reason: The saving is an aggregate departmental estimate over three years, not an attributable outcome.
No outcome for claimants or taxpayers beyond the aggregate estimate is documented. Referred claimants bear an added evidence burden.

ai_role.statement: The NAO describes a model trained on historical fraud and error data that scores advance requests and refers those above a threshold. Every payment decision is made by a caseworker, so the model's contribution is prioritization. Developer and deployer are the same public body (DWP). The NAO, an independent auditor, wrote the report.

produced_by: A model trained on historical fraud and error data in advance claims. Referrals above a threshold are reviewed by caseworkers alongside control-group referrals with scores removed
must_hold: A human decision on every advance
Regular fairness assessments (age is the only protected characteristic in the model)
Feedback of review outcomes into the model

headline: Universal Credit advances model saves an estimated £4.4 million
metric: saving an estimated £4.4 million from 2022–23 to 2024–25 by DWP's estimate

comparator.against: a randomised control group sample of advance requests

later.note: DWP's effectiveness assessment for April 2025 to March 2026 found the retrained model 2.5 times more effective than a random control group and concluded it should keep operating.
later.quote: the model is 2.5 times more effective at identifying high-risk advances than a random control group, increasing the precision of referrals and enabling human decision-makers to focus on the riskiest cases

value.quote: DWP estimates that, from 2022-23 to 2024-25, the model generated savings of £4.4 million that would otherwise have been overpaid.
